speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: PROPOSED INCREASE IN PENALTIES FOR MARIJUANA USE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Minister of Justice whether in view of police statements made in the last couple of days regarding the explosive degree to which marijuana is being used in this country, consideration is being given by the government to bringing in legislation to increase the minimum penalty so there will be some deterrent to this very serious offence which is affecting the people of Canada in all the provinces.

subtopic: PROPOSED INCREASE IN PENALTIES FOR MARIJUANA USE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, such consideration is not being given, but action is being taken now by the courts to increase the deterrent. Whereas previously the courts had very often taken the view that on the first offence possession would be met with a suspended sentence, now the inclination of the courts is to give a prison sentence and sometimes impose a very heavy fine in addition, precisely in order to increase that deterrent.

subtopic: PROPOSED INCREASE IN PENALTIES FOR MARIJUANA USE
speechtext: Was a suggestion made to the courts that the giving of suspended sentences was not in the interests of the administration of justice, and did that come from the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED INCREASE IN PENALTIES FOR MARIJUANA USE
speechtext: On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the Department of Justice has taken the position that if the courts requested a recommendation, the department would not ordinarily suggest a suspended sentence but would ask the courts to consider the position which was stated by the court of appeal in British Columbia, that is the position I have just stated, that a first offence would not automatically be met with a suspended sentence.

subtopic: PROPOSED INCREASE IN PENALTIES FOR MARIJUANA USE
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I have also been given notice of this question by the hon. member for Halifax, and I have an answer I should like to give.
First of all with regard to the chief justices' meeting, a meeting was held last week of chief justices from all across Canada. Considerable progress was made. It is the intention
March 21, 1968	COMMONS
of the government to have the Divorce Act proclaimed and in force as soon as this can be done. However, in any event this cannot be before May 2 in view of section 27 of the act. There are a number of matters that have to be dealt with, including the ironing out of these rules and the establishment of exchequer courts where required. speechtext:
6c. Reimbursement of the Defence Production Revolving Fund established by section 16(1) of the Defence Production Act for losses sustained in the operation of the crown-owned magnesium foundry at Haley, Ontario, prior to its sale in December, 1967, $480,000.
March 21, 1968
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, as a result of inquiries I made since last night I am concerned about the closing of the Haley operation as a crown corporation and the other arrangements which followed. I am surprised and disappointed that the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek is not with us today because he raised a very important question in relation to this matter.
After looking at the act I am convinced that the minister was correct when he suggested that he had the right to make the arrangement he did but I am wondering whether the arrangement was appropriate. I drew the inference last night that there is a similarity between this operation and other crown corporations which could be sold in the same manner if the government so desired. I have never been satisfied about the method of sale engaged in by the war assets corporation, later the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, in that it seems to be a wholesale operation. I realize it is difficult to retail an entire plant of this type. However, when certain of my constituents have wanted to purchase a jeep, a land rover or a Bren gun carrier to be used in a tourist operation they were informed they would be put on the list provided they could prove financial responsibility and were told that the equipment would be sold in blocks of perhaps 50 units. It does not seem to be in our interest to offer blocks of 50 Bren gun carriers, 20 Sherman tanks or other lots of equipment in this way. I suggest that the difficulties resulting from that type of sale are greater than the difficulties involved in selling single units at a reasonable price. While I agree that the minister has a right to make the arrangement he did, I am not sure we should operate on that basis.
The hon. member for Renfrew North made some very interesting observations and was obviously pleased that this plant was continuing in operation. I agree that it should continue to operate. But it seems to be strange that the corporation should sell this plant to a private operator and expect that operator to carry on the operation successfully without the advantages that a crown corporation would have, particularly when we realize that when the company was operated by the corporation it was unsuccessful.
From my own experience I can say that it is very difficult to establish an industry in
Supply-Defence Production either Renfrew North or Renfrew South and it has been very difficult to keep the industries going that were established there on a wartime basis. Most of these plants connected with the aircraft industry have been in difficulty ever since they changed over to peacetime production. It seems to me that a crown corporation would have a better chance of success because the government could direct certain purchase orders to that corporation. Purchases from private industries by the government must be done on a tender basis, or this reason I fail to understand the enthusiasm of the hon. member for Renfrew North in relation to the plant being turned over to a private operator on the basis of a very short term guarantee.
The minister was quite frank regarding land values and the potential in this area. We are all convinced that federal assistance will have to be given to maintain employment and the standard of living in this section of the country. While the minister has some responsibility in relation to the assistance provided in that area he is not involved as Minister of Defence Production in all the assistance programs. This area has a surplus of labour. We have been able to train highly skilled labour in specific areas of production who are capable of doing work such as is done in operations like de Havilland and in other areas where the Department of Defence Production has established operations with government subsidies to produce instruments and other things for the Department of National Defence.
It would have been wise for the hon. member for Renfrew North to have considered this whole operation in terms of a government contribution to the area to help maintain the labour force there. Surely a crown corporation could adapt to the changing circumstances if a private operator can do so in this area. The new company is required to operate for two years and it will be operating in exactly the same field and with the same facilities as the Haley operation.
It has been suggested that the plant and the machinery are quite old and that the operation is antiquated. Apparently the plant cannot be modified in order to perform some other function than that for which it was designed. If this is the case it would seem to me that the hon. member is very shortsighted in not looking at what has developed in other areas and realizing that this type of operation must have assistance and must have government orders.

March 21, 1968
Supply-Defence Production [DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Let me refer to an operation in my area as an example of what I have in mind. There has been a large foundry in my area for some time. It was developed some 25 years ago under the aegis of the British government. A young engineer was sent out from England to look after the Wabi iron works. He was sent out on the basis of either making the plant a paying proposition in two years or closing it down. He came out, looked at the foundry and decided it could be made a paying proposition. Through some managerial arrangement he eventually became the owner of the plant and it developed into one of the largest foundries in Ontario.
The aging of the plant and other considerations led him to decide to sell it and he did so to Canada Foundries (Wabi) Limited. For 25 years the plant operated in the foundry business on a full time basis. Very seldom was there a lay-off at the plant. If there was a lay-off it was always occasioned by a changeover in the operations of the plant. Continuous employment was provided for the people working at the plant. When it was sold this year Canada Foundries took into consideration their over-all operation and decided that they had to lay off people somewhere. Where did they lay them off? They were laid off at the Wabi plant at New Liskeard. For the first time in the operation of the plant most of the employees were laid off on a short term basis which stretched beyond what was anticipated in the initial stages. There is now some doubt about the efficiency and continued operation of the plant.
I also draw to the attention of the hon. member for Renfrew North the fact that we had in New Liskeard a pea-canning factory. Northern Ontario, particularly the clay belt of Timiskaming, produces the best peas in the world. Our peas have been exhibited at the Toronto Exhibition, the Royal Winter Fair and the World Exhibition in Chicago. We took top honours for the production of peas and therefore I can safely say that we grow the best peas in the world.
That plant had very good sales in the limited field in which it operated and this came to the attention of Canada Packers because of competition. Canada Packers bought the plant and within two years shut it down. They did not close it down because the plant was necessarily antiquated, although they said it was. They did not close it down because of its limited production which was serving a need. It was not closed down because we did not

have the best product on the North American continent but simply because the plant did not fit into their trading pattern. It did not fit into their corporate practice.
I suggest that the hon. member for Renfrew North is very shortsighted if he does not consider what has happened in other areas and does not realize that private industry is in no way capable of taking advantage of dealing with the Department of Defence Production to the extent that a crown corporation can. We have an obligation to the people of Renfrew North. We established a crown corporation plant in the town of Haley. It is true that the plant is not right in the town but the town of Haley exists only because of Haley Industries. It is situated on a railway and is a small community. Its only purpose is as a shopping facility for those employed at Haley Industries and local farmers.
The employment picture of the people who live there and have been trained there has been presented to us. It appears that most of the employees can be considered permanent and have served with the company for some time. It seems to me that we have an obligation to keep the plant in operation.
The minister is also in charge of the area development plan. He is the minister responsible for the development of secondary industry in areas where such industry has not been provided. It seems to me that a changeover from a government operated plant to one operated by private enterprise is a step backward, not a step forward. I challenge the minister to rise and say that anyone has challenged the deficits which Haley Industries has had over the years. It was not aware that it had been a crown corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: It was not.

That is a debatable point because I am of the opinion that it had the same kind of relationship enjoyed by crown corporations. As I understand the definition applied to Polymer, for example, would apply in much the same way to Haley Industries. However, that does not matter to my argument. I may be wrong semantically.
I make this argument not to the minister but to the hon. member for Renfrew North. The crown took this step because of necessity, not because of any desire to become involved in the establishment of plants. I am fully aware that if there are to be new plants in northern Ontario or Renfrew North they will have to be sponsored by the crown and receive assistance from the crown.
March 21. 1968

One of the problems in this regard is the very thing that the minister said caused the demise of this plant, namely, our grave inability to supply entrepreneurial acumen. I have heard people in northern Ontario talk about what they would do if they had $1 million to invest. There are in my part of northern Ontario hundreds of millions of dollars which could be invested. They play the stock market every day with that kind of money. The town next to the one from which I come at one time during the depression had less than 2,000 inhabitants but 13 millionaires. So the people of Haileybury could probably put up an immense amount of capital to build plants provided personnel were available to decide what types of industry were best suited to the area and to operate them.
In my opinion this is what is wrong with the area development program. We do not know what we have to sell and we would not know how to run the business even if we could sell the product. We therefore follow the old practice of establishing industries in major cities where there are closer and more extensive markets, and the small plants in the hinterland fall by the wayside. If this plant served a purpose for the Department of Defence Production, that purpose is probably as useful today as it was in the initial stages.
Under the National Research Council there are a large number of projects which will be brought to fruition if plants and trained people are available. I remember listening not long ago to the national research people talking about this very problem. They said they had developed a particular process that they thought was a "first" in the world. They looked around for people to operate in the field but had to get American companies to operate the project because no Canadian company would do so.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
There are still free enterprisers in the government. There are free enterprisers in the minister's department, because I am certain that the whole operation of the area development program is carried out on a free enterprise basis. We are giving assistance in this field. But I am sure there are also other people who are shocked at the fact that so much interest is shown in closing down crown corporations when the obvious need for them has disappeared. Everyone can remember when the Polymer corporation went around asking various rubber companies to take over their operation. I understand that Polymer was offered to the Firestone company for $1 after

Supply-Defence Production the war. If we had 100 Polymer corporations the Minister of Finance would now have less difficulty in balancing the budget because this corporation is making an unusually large profit. Its operations have been of advantage to Canada because the company developed a totally new process for making synthetic rubber which is being used in many countries and is of great potential value to us.
I am not too familiar with mouldings and castings, nor do I understand why the Haley plant found it necessary to tie itself to the production of a particular aircraft engine. But I do think that the Department of National Defence should decide that a certain amount of business should be directed to this plant, and I suggest that if this is not done now the Bartaco company will not be successful.
It seems to me that the hon. member representing that area should forget about his desire and the desire of the department to establish a free enterprise operation and should think in terms of the development of an industry in his area which will have the effect of bringing about secondary industries around the primary development. Obviously castings must be used on something and for something, and they create a demand for raw materials. A plant which would use the raw materials available in the area is sufficient justification for its existence. If the whole machinery of the Department of Defence Production cannot be directed toward developing this plant to meet the current needs of the department, then I think the department has failed to justify its usefulness.
I do not know whether it was ever intended that the Department of Defence Production should enter into manufacturing. I am aware of the buying potential of the department, not only for the Department of National Defence but for all departments of the government. However, the Department of Defence Production has never really looked at industrial development in Canada in terms of the distribution of the Canadian potential and Canadian needs. We have purchasing needs in Canada, and I do not think that the sole responsibility of the Department of Defence Production is to do the purchasing. Its responsibility lies also in the distribution of the purchasing all across the country. So far as the part of northern Ontario which I represent is concerned, I suggest that the Department of Defence Production makes no purchases at all from primary producers there. None of the paper which the department purchases comes from primary producers but
March 21, 1968

Supply-Defence Production rather is purchased from agents of paper companies after it leaves the pulp and paper mills. Even that primary product is not purchased by the department for the needs of the government.
I am very surprised at the attitude of the hon. member for Renfrew North in agreeing to the closing down of the plant. When the plant closes down at the end of the contract two years from now, as no doubt it will, it will likely be integrated into the over-all operation of Bartaco and its principals and there will be no further need for the development of these castings. The money they have made will go into the amalgamation of the whole operation and little consideration will be given to the people in north Renfrew who will be laid off.
I think the hon. member's attitude is very shortsighted and is limited to taking advantage of the present opportunity. I suggest to him that he reconsider his attitude and become more concerned with the development of a number of plants in the area with the assistance of the government. I am very familiar with the difficulties several of these plants are facing and the fact that the low wages of the people in this area are the only thing that has made it possible for a large number of the plants in Renfrew to stay in operation in towns such as Arnprior, Pembroke and adjacent communities. Were it not for the fact that the wages of these people are 40 or 50 cents below the provincial level these plants would not be able to stay in operation. I suggest that the subsidization of these plants by the workers is not the correct method of keeping the plants in production.
It would be my wish, and perhaps the wish of other members of the house, that this matter be referred for study to a standing committee of the house. I do not disagree with the minister's policy in this respect but I doubt that this is the kind of operation in which the government should be involved. I have not had the opportunity to ascertain why this plant was started 40 years ago but I surmise that it operated for a number of years under the Department of Defence Production for the purpose of manufacturing specific commodities.
I am familiar to a certain extent with the difficulties in the production of aircraft faced by Sperry of Ottawa and a number of other plants in the Ottawa area. I am aware of the fact that these companies were subsidized to some degree and that they have continued to receive subsidies since they have ceased
[Mr. Peters.)
major production of aircraft. I am also aware of the operations of the de Havilland company and the fact that the company's operation in Toronto was developed for the purpose of building the Avro Arrow. When that program was scrapped, we not only lost an industry but we lost the potential ability to develop an aircraft industry. In my opinion we had a sufficient number of engineers in Canada. For a number of years I was in the ferry squadron in the air force. We had types of aircraft which were flown by the United States and British air forces and I had an opportunity to see the inside and the outside of those planes. I am of the opinion that no other plane flying at that time could have outclassed the Avro Arrow. We brought the best people from England and we were able to encourage them to come here and build the basis for an aircraft industry which should have put Canada in the forefront.
We are all familiar with the story of Avro Arrow in which both fact and fancy are involved. There is no point in going over it. The fact is that we lost an industry and the potential for an aircraft industry.

Mr. Chairman, the consideration of the estimates of this department gives us an opportunity to comment on the expenditure of very large sums of money. How significant some of these sums of money are was very well summarized in the leading editorial of this morning's Globe and Mail in which it was pointed out that the four new destroyers the department has on its drawing boards will cost some $200 million or, as the paper says, about $50 million more than the Minister of Finance hopes to raise by the recent 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporation income taxes. This is certainly a very significant sum of money, particularly in the light of the urging by the same government which proposes to spend it that Canadians use restraint in their own spending. Can you imagine the reaction of the working people of Canada, the pensioners or, for that matter, the business people, when they learn that the government which is asking them to "cool it" proposes to spend some $200 million on what I believe to be questionable vessels of war?
March 21. 1968

[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I say "questionable vessels" because as is reported these ships were first conceived four years ago. They were to be part of the new integrated defence equipment program. These vessels were to be the first surface to air missile equipped destroyers to meet our NATO requirements. They were designed four years ago and apparently will be in operation four years hence. In the meanwhile we have not really redefined our NATO responsibilities.
This is a curious situation, Mr. Chairman. As I understand it, these boats were to have cost $20 million each. They are now estimated to cost $50 million each. If I may quote the Globe and Mail again, it says in the editorial:
In what strange unreal world does the government live, where It can preach restraint to us and proceed, almost casually, with a huge and open-ended expenditure on what the judgment of Canadians-if it could be totalled up-would almost certainly decide was an unnecessary and even undesirable project?
I think that is a very good question, a $200 million question. There is another aspect of the Department of Defence Production in which I am sure many Canadians are interested. I refer to our defence production sharing agreement with the United States. My colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood, recently made what I thought was an excellent presentation of his views regarding the position of Canada in supplying war materials to be used in Viet Nam. As he said, the original agreement to share defence production with the United States was of some benefit to Canada. It gave Canadian firms a share in the production of military equipment used by the United States.
Certainly it was natural for Canada to enter into this type of agreement with a close ally. However, Canada is not and cannot be an ally of the United States in Viet Nam. As my colleague suggested, it is time Canada had a new look at that agreement. It may be necessary for us to assert control over the export of war materials which no doubt will be used in Viet Nam. We have, of course, already limited the export of Canadian war materials to another NATO ally, Portugal, because we feared they would be used against African states rather than for NATO purposes.
There is one other aspect of defence production contracts which I should like to mention. A while ago the Financial Post contained an article in which it was stated:
Continued high Viet Nam war spending by the U.S. will keep up the big flow of contracts and orders to Canadian companies for both military and civilian goods.
Supply-Defence Production
Of course, some plants in the United States are so busy with war production that they have to give civilian production to other plants. The Financial Post article continues:
The question is this ... is additional Viet Nam related production in Canadian plants more than offset by the adverse effects of war spending on the Canadian economy as a whole?
In so far as inflation is concerned, Viet Nam was responsible for one-third of the rise in consumer prices in the United States last year. Certainly the effect of this has carried over into our own country. It seems to me that Canada's relationship to United States defence contracts is something like that of the man who warms his hands at the fire of a neighbour. It is very comfortable at times but, as is well known, as well as having a capacity to warm fire also has the capacity to burn and scorch. I think we should be very much aware of this capacity. It is surely not exhibiting friendship for the United States for us to go along with the policy on Viet Nam of the present United States administration, a policy that is costing billions of dollars and thousands of lives. In my view this policy also leaves the United States open to possible weakness to attack from other sources.
I believe that the defence production sharing agreement with the United States gives Canada the opportunity to express her opposition, and I am sure that opposition exists in many Canadian households, to being considered an ally of the United States in a dangerous, hopeless and very costly mistake. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I invite the minister to comment on the remarks I have made, particularly those involving the quotations from the Globe and Mail and the Financial Post.

I will try to be brief, Mr. Chairman, but there are certain aspects of the operations of this department to which I feel I must make reference before the vote carries. I wonder whether the minister would care to deny the charge that in its operations the Department of Defence Production shows a very strong regional bias? Last year I put a question on the order paper inquiring as to what proportion of defence production contracts had been allocated to firms in the four western provinces of Canada. The reply indicated that the four western provinces, which have 25 per cent of the population of the country, received only 8 per cent of the total value of contracts let by the department.
March 21. 1988

Supply-Defence Production
Of course the minister may have a very facile reply to that charge. He may say it so happens that most of the industries set up for the production of goods such as weapons systems, and so on, happen to be located in other parts of the country. The fact is, however, that I am referring to the total value of contracts let by the department, not just for weapons systems but also for ordinary, less sophisticated parts, supplies, clothing, food and so on. It seems to me there is no point in overlooking the fact that for years now, out of $700 million or $800 million per year of prime contracts let by the Department of Defence Production an inordinately small proportion has been placed in western Canada.
Some of the contracts, of course, are let under the bid system, so the answer will be that firms in eastern Canada are bidding lower prices. This answer would not cover the whole point because many of the contracts let by the department are on a cost plus basis and some are on the basis of a bid with a clear stipulation for adjustment for unforeseen expenses. However, I believe it is clear the Department of Defence Production is allocating to the four western provinces, containing 25 per cent of the population, contracts representing only 8 per cent of the total value of contracts let by the department. The situation may vary from year to year, but I challenge the minister to show that it varies greatly.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I think it is a mixed blessing for a regional economy to have to depend on defence production industries, because they have undesirable side effects. Defence production industries do bring considerable employment and, through the multiplier effect, considerable indirect employment to a community. Many industries grow out of defence production which can transfer their operations to non-military production. Industries high in research and development content grow up around defence production industries and certainly that does no harm to any regional economy. However, as I said, there are certain undesirable side effects in that regions of the country that depend heavily on defence production industries have, to use a colloquial expression, a tiger by the tail.
In the course of the past two or three months most hon. members have received a pamphlet containing reprints from the Financial Post which indicate that the war in Viet Nam is doing wonders for Canadian business

and the Canadian economy. This is particularly the case in those regions of the country that are heavily dependent on defence production industries. Since 1963-64 there has been virtually a 100 per cent increase in the amount of defence production exports to the United States. According to the pamphlet the minister is quoted as saying that defence production contracts in 1966 resulted in full time employment of between 13,000 and 15,000 Canadians, and that an additional 110,000 persons are estimated to be affected indirectly as a result of contracts to ship that materiel to the United States.
Without getting into the philosophical ramifications of the war in Viet Nam, Mr. Chairman, I know all hon. members hope and pray that very soon it will be ended. However, I should like to ask the minister what contingency plans his department and the government are making to take care of those employees who will be directly and immediately affected by the cessation of hostilities in Viet Nam and thereby faced with a prospective loss of employment. Plants producing such materiel are geared to full and overtime production. But when the war is over they will be working at less than full production, either on a part shift basis or on a slow shift basis. Some will be on the verge of closure. Although we all hope and pray the war will soon be over, there are thousands of people who are depending on the war for their livelihood and I should like to ask what contingency plans exist to meet the decrease in production on the termination of the war. I suspect that not very much is being done about the matter.
Some continue to express great enthusiasm over the fact that our defence production sales to the United States have been surging upward so dramatically in the past two years. I am not questioning the defence production sharing agreement between Canada and the United States. The country to the south has been our ally over the decades. At one time Franklin Roosevelt referred to that country as the arsenal of democracy, and that is still my view.
During the first few years of the life of the defence production sharing agreement both countries benefited mutually. However, we now find ourselves in a situation where we must not only look at the direct economic benefits but also at the moral and philosophical implications of the war. We have got ourselves into a hopeless position. Rather than take the time of the committee at this
March 21. 1968

stage to berate the minister for something about which I concede there is very little of a tangible nature he can do at the moment to correct, I do accuse him and his colleagues of complacency if they are not now actively engaged in the drawing up of contingency plans so that people who are adversely affected by the cessation of hostilities in Viet Nam will be quickly accommodated with alternative employment.
I am sure the minister is aware that when former President Dwight Eisenhower made his farewell address to the nation, I believe in late 1960 or early 1961, surprisingly enough for an old professional soldier he took the opportunity to warn his fellow citizens about the very real danger that was poised to strike at the heart of democracy in the United States. He was referring to the danger created by the large and growing military-industrial complex, as he put it, in the United States. This complex, was getting so powerful that not only representatives in the state legislatures but some of the congressmen who represented areas of the nation heavily dependent upon defence production of munitions and armaments were being influenced to the point that they could hardly take a position other than one of support for more and more defence and armaments production.
I realize that it is not considered to be good taste to refer in this chamber to public personages in other countries, certainly not if one feels compelled to make critical comments about them. Therefore I will not mention any names. However, I think hon. members will agree with me when I say that many of the elected representatives in the United States do take a stance with respect to defence and foreign policy that might be roughly described as hawkish. It should also be noted that in most cases these same people represent areas of the United States that are heavily dependent upon the production of armaments and munitions.
When I was at the NATO conference in Brussels last fall I had occasion to get to know a distinguished United States congressman with flowing white hair who took such a hawkish position on most of the major issues then being discussed that even his colleagues were somewhat dismayed. I did not regard it as a coincidence that he happened to represent a particular region of one state which, if it had had one more defence production industry added to those already there, would have likely sunk into the Atlantic ocean.
Supply-Defence Production [DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Our defence production industry is much smaller, but we must resolve to plan our economy so that no region of this country will ever need to turn to defence production to give its inhabitants a livelihood. Western Canada, with its relatively abundant natural resources and fertile soil, does not much need industries which depend on armament production, though I suspect that other areas of the country which are not so lucky depend on armament production to give their inhabitants employment.
I hope that no minister of the crown will continue to wax enthusiastic, as some ministers have in the past 12 months, about increased arms exports to the United States resulting from the Viet Nam war. We are selling arms to the United States because of an agreement we feel bound to adhere to. Let us hope, for everybody's sake, that the war will soon end. If it does not, I suggest we ought to consider the desirability of terminating the export to the United States of materiel that is used directly in Viet Nam.
For the past two years, because I have been confused about the United States' role in Viet Nam I have not criticized United States' actions. I wondered how that country's determination to resist aggression could be balanced against the killing of innocent bystanders. Despite motives which I do not question, the war in Viet Nam by degrees has become genocide. This has been unintentional, but even intended actions often bring strange results. I am sure that when United States military advisers were sent to Viet Nam a few years ago they were sent to help the South Vietnamese resist aggression. By degrees the war has escalated and now it has become an exercise in genocide.
In Canada we say to the United States: Stop the bombing, do this and do that. While we continue to sell vital war materials to the United States-and this is germane to this discussion-we are in a poor position to criticize. As a matter of fact, I question our right to criticize United States actions. I agree with the United States senator who said yesterday in a public statement, while discussing positions that could be taken about the Viet Nam war, that Canada cannot criticize because she is benefiting directly from war material sales.
Yesterday the hon. members for Swift Current-Maple Creek and Rosthern spoke about the sale of the crown owned magnesium foundry at Haley, Ontario. I have not time to say

Supply-Defence Production everything I should like to about that transaction but I understand from the remarks of the hon. member for Renfrew North that the industry in question is essential for the economic well-being of his region. When he accused members of the Conservative party, the hon. members for Swift Current-Maple Creek and Rosthern in particular, of speaking against the interests of his district he was being silly. No one on this side of the chamber suggested that the industry should be closed down. We question the prudence and business judgment shown by the crown in disposing of this foundry to a privately owned company.
Though the terms of sale are somewhat cloudy, one gathers that this crown owned industry had accounts receivable of about $250,000 and inventory of about the same amount. For those assets the private company paid what? It is difficult to come to a concrete conclusion from the minister's words but I suspect the plant was sold for the nominal sum of $1. Though the terms are not clear it appears that in return for the inventory and accounts receivable the new owners had to pledge that the plant would be kept in operation for two years.
Significantly, the sale conditions do not prevent the purchaser from selling the foundry to a second party which in turn may sell it to a third party. I suspect that to the purchasing company this transaction represented a capital gain, one of those finagling little deals. I see no other reason for their getting involved in an industry the crown was anxious to get rid of. There is some onus on the minister to be more explicit than he was yesterday when he tried to answer questions asked by the hon. members for Swift Current-Maple Creek and Rosthern.
When the industry in question started losing money five years ago, surely the Department of Defence Production must have known that some day soon the plant would have to be closed down or sold. Why was there no contingency planning in 1963, 1964 or 1965? Why were plant operations allowed to go blithely along? Then, because the hon. member representing the area became concerned, as well he should, certain representations were made. The crown then enters into a deal with this private company on strange, almost incomprehensible terms of sale. The company takes possession and it has to keep the plant operating for two years but it need not remain as owner. I agree with my hon. friend from Timiskaming that the region of
[Mr. Schreyer.J

Renfrew North would have been much better served had the crown been kept in the picture, had the plant been kept operational by the crown or the crown had been responsible for transforming the operation into an operation of a different type.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
There is one other aspect. The crown made this sale on generous terms. Can the minister tell us whether the company which purchased this foundry will be applying to the Department of Industry for grants under AIDA and PAIT? If such grants are made it seems to me the benevolence of the crown will have been compounded in favour of a group of entrepreneurs who 1 suspect went into this venture for the sake of capital gain. The people of Renfrew North deserve something better than to be left at the mercy of private monopolies such as this.

Mr. Chairman, I have for a long time felt it was time somebody in Canada attempted to take the self-applied wool from our eyes in connection with the whole question of defence production and expenditures. It is unfortunate that human beings appear to need comforting myths by which to live even though those myths lead in the end to their own destruction. In Canada we are loath to accept the real facts of our position in the world today when it comes to military expenditures.
I have watched two wars in my lifetime and taken part in one. I am observing now, as everybody else is doing, the progress of another war which has been condemned on all sides both in the United States and in the rest of the world. Yet we seem unable to draw lessons for our own policies in this regard from the harsh facts of modern warfare. It is estimated that the United States is spending some $30 billion to prosecute the war in Viet Nam. I suggest that in this context Canada and countries with similar resources can have no part to play and that we should not delude ourselves into thinking there might be a quiet, conventional war in which Canada could play a significant part.
As my hon. friend from Springfield pointed out, the war in Viet Nam started out on the assumption that it was to be a brushfire war, a police action to stem the tide of communist revolution in Viet Nam. But things rapidly got out of hand and the conflict developed into a major war. I suspect that all wars
March 21. 1968

which are allowed to break out in the future will become major wars. There was a war in the Middle East recently which was not allowed to develop beyond a local conflict but it was more by luck than good guidance that the great powers were not involved in those hostilities which could have spread to the entire world.
I doubt whether there is anyone here who can tell me what particular advantage by way of defence Canada has received as a result of the defence expenditures which I have noted for the last 15 years since I first came to the House of Commons-sums running from $1J billion to $14 billion a year during that period. I have been waiting for some minister of defence to tell me convincingly that these expenditures have resulted in any greater safety for the Canadian people than would have been the case had we made them on other things in our economy or on helping people in underdeveloped countries. No one has been able to come up with a case for these expenditures. We are always told, usually in vague terms, about the dangers which confront us but we are never told how the measures Canada takes will contribute to warding off those dangers. The latest folly is the pretence that there is a threat of armed bombers attacking Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says he doubts whether anyone can give him a satisfactory answer to his question concerning the validity in terms of national security of expenditures made on defence. I think that is quite true. He will certainly have difficulty in getting an answer from me. But he will be provided with an opportunity later under item 16, when the estimates of the Department of National Defence are being considered, to put his question directly to the Minister of National Defence.

I gather the minister is suggesting that my remarks are inappropriate at this point. I would remind him that we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Defence Production which is tied in very closely with defence expenditure in general. So it seems to me the subject I have raised could be discussed on the estimates of either department.
Or on both.

Or on both, yes, though I would not presume to do that.
Supply-Defence Production
As the minister has admitted, no one is able to tell us with any conviction that we have gained any significant protection as a result of the expenditures we have made over the years. Why should we imagine there would be a reasonable argument in support of the policy we have been following? We have only to look at the quantities of material involved in a modern war to realize that Canada could play no part of any consequence in such an area.
I have been concerned about the attitude of a number of young men in our armed forces who feel ill at ease about the role in which they are cast, people who have a nagging suspicion that they are merely wasting their time and wasting the country's resources for no visible purpose. This is having a demoralizing effect on many of them. I have come across this attitude repeatedly in speaking to young men in the armed forces serving in various ranks. Perhaps they have a clearer picture of the situation than other Canadians have; they realize they have no part to play in the area of modern war.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
What are we defending ourselves against? The only thing we have to fear is the use of modern weapons of offence and those weapons, we have been repeatedly told, are not susceptible to defence action. I have heard of no way by which an attack by intercontinental guided missiles can be repulsed. The only possibility, and I submit it is only a bare possibility, is by having what was described by the inimitable Mr. Dulles as a massive deterrent. It may be true that the massive deterrent the United States has been building up has warded off an attack by these sophisticated modern weapons, although I somewhat doubt that. But even if that is the case it merely supports my argument that there is no role for Canada to play because any contribution we can make cannot add to the massive deterrent force now amassed by the United States.
To pretend we can contribute in any way whatever, let alone any significant way, is self-delusion. I suspect it is based on two things, one being the wishes of interested parties in Canada who seek gain from the expenditures we make on defence, and the other being that some people refuse to accept the fact, although they have been told it over and over again, that there is no defence. To me it is a tragedy that the Canadian people, in possession of such a vast quantity of
March 21, 1968

Supply-Defence Production resources, with such tremendous capacities, are content to waste their efforts on this sort of expenditure rather than really entering into the field that is demanding so much in the modern world, the development of the underdeveloped countries of the world.
I have a very clear recollection of the day in this house when it looked as though we were coming to the end of things. I refer, of course, to the confrontation over Cuba. I have been interested to note in all my reading of the discussions on the matter that no one goes farther back than the situation that obtained after Fidel Castro succeeded in seizing power in Cuba. No one goes farther back in history where there are another few links in the chain of cause and effect which finally led us that day in the House of Commons to sit here wondering whether we were facing the end of all things. If people would go farther back they would find something else that Canada and other prosperous parts of the world should not be very proud of, namely, that for decades we had known that the Cuban people were suffering under one of the most brutal dictatorships in the history of the world. They were living in poverty, in misery and in fear, and we did nothing about it. As a consequence the chain of events led finally to the confrontation between the two great powers in the world.
I suggest that if we are interested in our own defence we should be bending all our efforts to coping with all the potential Cubas that exist throughout the world which may at any time produce the chain of cause and effect that will lead us to the brink of disaster. I can think of no more honourable, no more decisive and significant role for Canada at this time than to say to the rest of the world that we are not interested in this fatal game of military expenditures and military defiance because we know we can play no real role in it. We should say that we want to free our hands to undertake the task that lies ahead of all of us in the more affluent parts of the world, which is to remove to the best of our ability the causes of future disruption of peace in the world by removing the poverty and misery underlying those causes. But if we are going to go on playing, which is all we are doing-posturing, playing and pretending-that we in Canada can play any sort of role whatsoever in the military sense we are not going to have the resources, the energies and the time to engage in the real peace keeping operation of trying to build up the

submerged areas of the world to the level of affluence that we enjoy on this continent.
I cannot think of anything that would enhance the prestige of Canada and Canadians more than if tomorrow Canada were to announce to the world: This is the end, we are going to spend no more on useless military expenditures; we are taking steps within our own country to develop our own economy and labour force whereby we can make a massive contribution to world development. Canadians would then have reason to be proud of the role Canada was playing in the world. I have little reason to be proud of a people who through vanity, through pride, call it what you will, want to go on pretending and posturing that they cut some ice in the military world of today. Who wants to? Who wants to play in this evil game? I think that sensible people, responsible people, would be happy to see Canada withdraw from it, and throughout the world there would be other peoples and other nations who would draw a breath of relief that finally in one part of the world the light of common sense was prevailing and the follies of the past were finally being put behind us.

Mr. Chairman, against the kind of background established by the speeches of the hon. member for Springfield and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands I would like to take a few minutes of the committee's time to pinpoint the impact of some of the things they have been saying upon a particular area of Canada and the people of that area.
The hon. member for Springfield, said it was fortunate that in not too many places in western Canada were the people basically dependent upon the defence program and the establishments that exist because we have a Department of Defence Production and supply what some people once would have called our war machine and which some of us in this chamber have heard described as our peace machine. I happen to have a community of that kind in my constituency and whenever I listen to discussion of the estimates of a department like the Department of Defence Production I immediately think of these constituents who are in a very vulnerable position.
I do not know whether it is ironic or a hopeful sign that the Minister of Defence Production has another hat. He is also known as the Minister of Industry. There are many of
March 21. 1968

us who are hopeful that some day he will be able to discard one of his hats and devote his entire energy to the Department of Industry. I am not restricting this observation merely to the present incumbent of this office but rather have in mine a future organization of the departments of the government of Canada which I would like to see take place. Nevertheless I feel that the remarks made by the hon. members for Springfield and Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands have clearly set out the fact that the minister's dual functions are so intertwined that they cannot really be separated. While one may hope that one area of his responsibility will be phased out and that the other will increase, nevertheless at this moment we are dealing with the estimates for the current fiscal year and therefore have to be concerned primarily with the present situation.
The concern I have expressed about the situation in which these constituents of mine find themselves is not wholly mine but is widely shared by many of the residents of the area. I would like to refer to a brief circulated by the Courtenay-Comox chamber of commerce around the end of last year in which some attention is focused on the situation in which the ordinary citizens, business people and professional people in that area find themselves. The brief points out the following:
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Over the last ten years in the Comox valley we have seen a gradual decline in the number of wage earners in the logging and woods industries until today this payroll is estimated to be less than 500.
I might interpolate here and say that during an earlier era the basic industry in the area was coal mining but apparently what has been happening in Cape Breton happened there. One of the economic bases of this community has been non-existent now for quite a number of years. Logging and other forest production industries were available and perhaps in some measure eased the blow when coal mining ceased to a greater extent than the blow in Cape Breton is being eased. I point out to the minister that the decline in the number of wage earners arises in part from changing technology in the forest industry. This means that more logs can be produced with fewer people. The brief then continues:
Farming has shown a steady decline in employment opportunities and many of the small farmers have to supplement their income with other employment.

I do not see the Minister of Agriculture here so I can do nothing but ask the Minister of Defence Production to make note of that for his colleague's benefit. The brief then states:
Against this there has been a steady increase in the number of wage earners who are directly dependent on the Canadian Forces Base, Comox, for their income.
A great deal of the money that the minister supervises has been spent in this area, as I am sure the minister will agree. Farther on in the brief it is pointed out:
In summary we have reached a situation where an estimated amount of between 60 per cent and 70 per cent of the total income in the area is directly dependent on the Department of National Defence base at Comox. This places our economy in a very vulnerable position should there be any change in D.N.D. policies in the future which might lead to retrenchment and a cut-back in defence spending. At the moment there is no alternative or additional source of payroll income in sight for this area and it is considered that urgent action is necessary to remedy this deficiency and to attract more sources of employment to the Comox Valley.
The brief then goes on to detail the efforts made over the past 15 years or so by the local body to stimulate other industrial development in the area. I will not go into that in detail. However, in responding to this brief and the covering letter I said to the people of the Comox-Courtenay chamber of commerce:
While I do not know of any current planning of the government in the defence field which is likely to alter in a major way the functioning of Canadian Forces Base Comox on its current scale, I have long been concerned about the increasing vulnerability of the economy of your area to any change which would eliminate or reduce the present establishment, on top of which I am sure there are none of us who do not hope for a state of affairs in the world where that kind of an stab-lishment will become redundant.
I might say for the benefit of the minister and the committee that what I had in mind when I used that last phrase was redundant as far as the thinking of the government of Canada is concerned.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands very ably developed the idea that basically our defence effort is a redundant operation at the present time. I share this view and I have made that clear on more than one occasion when I have addressed audiences in the area. In other words, the plain fact of the matter is that the spending of the number of millions of dollars supervised by the Minister of Defence Production
March 21, 1968

Supply-Defence Production represents a wasteful expenditure of Canadian taxpayers' money, to say nothing of any other considerations regarding the future of the world. Be that as it may, I do not believe that a view has so far been held by the Minister of National Defence or the Minister of Defence Production who is responsible for the spending of some of this money. From any indication we have had, even from some of the more hopeful of the aspirants to the office of the Prime Minister, it is not likely that there will be any basic change in policy on the part of the Canadian government as long as the party across the way remains in office.
The Minister of Defence Production should be reminded that he has another hat. We welcomed the establishment of the Department of Industry. I am sure the minister knows the terms of reference which set him up as the Minister of Industry much better than most members of the committee. Section 7 sets out some of the responsibilities and along others it states that he should promote the establishment, growth, efficiency and improvement of manufacturing industries in Canada, and develop and carry out such programs and projects as may be appropriate. He is concerned with spending money as Minister of Defence Production but I would urge upon him that he be even more concerned about fulfilling his other role and that he should not lose sight of the fact that his operations and those of his colleague, the Minister of National Defence, have placed whole segments of the Canadian population in a very vulnerable economic position.
Even in the minister's new role as Minister of Industry there has been no real assurance from anything that has happened so far that the federal government has taken any real initiative to ensure that an alternative economic base for this community is being developed to counterbalance the vulnerable situation in which the community finds itself because it is dependent on the defence establishment. This is true of other places where the people are more directly dependent on the defence manufacturing field.
Even though the minister is sitting here at the moment as the Minister of Defence Production I should like to point out that I recognize his other role. I have made inquiries of the area development agency of the Department of Industry and have been assured of the willingness of that agency to co-operate with the local people if they wish to set up an industry commissioner. I was
[Mr. BarnettJ
told that the appropriate officer of the department, a man who has spent some time in British Columbia, will do everything he can.
As the minister knows, we have had recent discussions about the question of designated areas, but this area does not fall within that particular classification. Therefore, except for a little advice and counselling in his role as Minister of Industry, the minister, as far as I can ascertain, has not really done very much to bring forward policies with any meaningful weight in relation to the provisions of the act for the purpose of developing and carrying out such programs and projects as may be appropriate. I suggest to him that he should not lose sight of this.
The minister quite properly suggested to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that we might be dealing with defence department estimates later. I agree that if I have questions to ask in relation to changes, if any, to be made in respect of this establishment they should properly be directed to the Minister of National Defence. I do not mind saying that I have discussed these matters on occasion with the minister and I am not asking him to answer at this time any of my questions relating to possible changes in the actual establishment.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a number of questions have been asked to which I shall try to give brief answers. The allegation was made that the cost of the d.d.h.'s had risen overnight. The evidence cited in support of this argument was an editorial which appeared in the current issue of a Toronto newspaper. I am sorry that the hon. gentleman who derived this information from the newspaper was not in the house when the question of costs was under discussion. At that time it was made clear that a number of figures had been bandied about in respect of naval construction which represented only parts of the total contract, that this had led to misunderstandings in the past and it was my intention to see that whenever questions relating to costs or estimates of costs for naval construction were asked the full cost would be provided on each occasion in addition to the costs asked for.
The hon. member for Springfield suggested that a regional bias was evident on the part 27053-4971
DEBATES	7897
Supply-Defence Production of the Department of Defence Production and this bias was given effect to by the use of cost plus contracts or contracts with adjustments for unforeseen circumstances. I suggest that cost plus contracts or contracts carrying-and I am not too clear what the hon. member meant by this-clauses for adjustment due to unforeseen circumstances, are rather unusual. I cannot think of one in which we are currently engaged.
It is the practice and policy of the department to seek to purchase by way of tender, based on the specifications and stated delivery times, and to award the contract to the lowest tenderer capable of meeting the terms of the tender. This in itself will serve to distribute in quite an automatic way the majority of contracts to those areas where most production is carried out. It is quite obvious that if a very small fraction of the total Canadian production is performed in a given area of Canada a correspondingly small number of contracts will emanate from the Department of Defence Production to that particular area.
In respect of the prairies, I think it is well known that the density of manufacturing there is much lower in relation to the population of the area than it is in other parts of Canada, notably Ontario, Quebec, the man-times and British Columbia. I might tell the hon. gentlemen, however, that the policy of consolidation of purchases and awarding the contract to the lowest tenderer, rather than making individual purchases locally, has resulted in the department being able to fulfil in quite a substantial way one of the main functions for which it was set up, namely, the acquisition of goods and services for the government of Canada at the lowest economical price.
As a consequence of the consolidation of fine paper requirements and seeking tenders for these in bulk, in the past year in respect of one kind of paper only, namely, No. 7 bond, a saving of $500,000 was achieved compared with previous purchasing practices, where this item was purchased on a frequent, repetitive and small quantity basis. By introducing a national credit card system for personnel in civilian departments to obtain gasoline, oil and minor repairs to government vehicles, annual savings estimated at $158,000 a year have been achieved. By introducing government-wide rates for newspaper advertising, annual savings of about $200,000 have been brought about.

Supply-Defence Production [DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
We are now continuing this consolidation operation in respect of advertising in other media and we hope to be able to reflect corresponding savings in this field. As members will recollect from a discussion we had last year on defence production estimates, through the policy of consolidating government needs for motor vehicles into a single purchase contract and by seeking tenders directly from the manufacturer, the department realized savings of between $100 and $400 per vehicle purchased.
I will not continue to give the many more examples of what I think the hon. gentleman has described as a bias in favour of certain areas in Canada, but I would say that the policy has had the result of concentrating purchasing in those areas where most of the production takes place. But while this concentration may have brought about some changes from previous practice I would point out that it has had the beneficial effect of effecting substantial savings in dollars to the taxpayers of Canada and that, I may say, is what I conceive my role as Minister of Defence Production to be.

I am sure the committee would be interested in having from the minister at this point an indication of the degree of purchasing on behalf of departments in relation to their requirements. Is his department purchasing 10 per cent, 50 per cent or most of the requirements for all government agencies? Perhaps he would also indicate how much of the purchasing is made in relation to defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
As recommended by the Glas-sco commission, purchasing for all departments is being consolidated on an orderly and progressive basis under the Department of Defence Production. We have been taking over departments in their entirety one at a time. If my memory serves me right, we are about half way through this process now. In another year and a half or two years' time I would hope the Department of Defence Production will be doing all the purchasing on a consolidated basis for all the departments and agencies of the government, with the exception of certain specialized purchasing related particularly to high technology, scientific disciplines, and research activities in which the researchers are much closer, both in terms of physical location, and certainly in terms of

intercommunication, with the source of supply, than a larger generalized department would be.
We are making satisfactory progress. In addition, there are some fields where we have taken over department by department and consolidated our policy in respect of certain commodities purchased for all government departments. Motor cars are one example, newspaper advertising is another, and stationery is still another. So in a sense we are going ahead in two directions and on two fronts, and this is being converted, I hope, into a coherent, integrated operation.
The hon. member for Springfield also asked what contingency plans were being made to look after people who would be unemployed as a consequence of a shrinkage of the consumption of materials produced in Canada now being used to support the war effort in Viet Nam. Let me say right away that I share fully his hope that this unfortunate conflict can be brought to a conclusion at the earliest possible moment and, along with my colleagues in the government, spare no effort to bring this about.
In so far as those who are engaged now in production related to current warlike operations are concerned, we have been consciously, so far as this is possible in a free enterprise society, endeavouring to see that no one firm becomes solely dependent on the production of articles of military use and military equipment for the armed forces. This is true whether the firm is producing solely for Canadian consumption or is producing also for other countries such as the United States, European countries, and others. We do what we can to produce a diversification from military equipment into appropriate related civilian lines so that, should the demand for military items of any kind and for any reason fall off, there will be an alternative to which to turn people's efforts from a base which we hope will be reasonably soundly established.
Perhaps I could cite some examples. Cana-dair, the firm manufacturing military aircraft such as the CF-5, both for Canada and for the Netherlands, has been encouraged by us to do research and development and even prototype construction work on aircraft which have a purely civilian role, the principal one of which would be for water bombing against forest fires. They are also concerned with research and development of vertical take-off aircraft, also for civilian purposes. This we endeavour to bring about in all those firms
March 21, 1968

with which we have contact, which are currently engaged in the production of items for the various departments of defence, Canadian and foreign.
I may say that from the point of view of the necessity for a substantial readjustment I think we in Canada are fortunate in one way in that the kinds of military equipment or components of military equipment on which Canadian firms have been concentrating are largely of a quasi-civilian character. An example of this is the doppler navigation system, a system of aerial navigation which was developed in Canada and is being manufactured here. It is essential for military operations and military aircraft. At the same time it is rapidly becoming very important in civil aircraft. So if for one reason or another the demand for doppler navigation equipment in military aircraft dries up, there will be an alternative civilian demand to be catered to which will continue to provide economic activities to these firms.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
We are conscious of the possibility and, we hope, the probability, that military operations with their consequent loss of life and material in Viet Nam will cease and have envisaged the circumstances of the changeover. We are working toward making it as reasonable and as easy as possible.
As I mentioned to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, I am sure the Minister of National Defence will read his remarks in Hansard and when the defence estimates are being considered it will not be necessary for him to repeat them. I leave it to my colleague the Minister of National Defence to make an adequate response.

speechtext: I am sorry, but the hon. gentleman was not in the house when I did refute it. Perhaps if he looks at Hansard he will see the answer.

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will permit an interruption, there is one other operation which I forgot, and which Canadian Arsenals owned. This is an establishment for the manufacture of cartridge cases at Louise Basin in Quebec. It is currently being operated by a contractor which is the same firm that purchased the arsenal at Valcartier, Val-cartier Industries Limited. Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the minister's statement that his department was giving considerable attention to the problem of changing from wartime products to peacetime products and that they had been looking at the various factors. Can we take it from this statement that the transition from the production of war material to peacetime products can be made easily and without serious disruption?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Easy, Mr. Chairman, is a relative term. Whether something is easy, whether dislocation is major or minor, whether it is easy or difficult, depends a lot on where you sit. If you were a man who had been gainfully employed in a job for a great many years and it suddenly disappeared, then it would be very difficult for you as an individual. However, if there is only one such instance in a year in the country, then that could hardly be regarded as a national problem. Such a transition would be easy for the government of Canada, indeed even easy for the opposition, but it would be very difficult indeed for that one man. I was endeavouring to say that the problem of transition is not a major one and we are seized of the importance of it. We are continuously taking steps to facilitate this transition on the day that we hope will come.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I mentioned to the hon. member for Timis-kaming the sale to Valcartier Industries Limited of Canadian Arsenals ammunitions producing plant at Valcartier. As a consequence of this, the crown has been able to secure the continuance in being of an ammunition producing facility to meet the needs

of the Department of National Defence. At the same time, by introducing an entrepreneurial management with other interests, the plant and machinery at Valcartier are being used not only for the production of small arms ammunition on a limited scale, which is all we need now, but for the manufacture of another range of both plastic and metal items. As a result, when the day arrives that small arms ammunition is no longer required, the plant at Valcartier and its employees will already be well launched into the production of civilian goods.

The importance of the minister's statement at this time, Mr. Chairman, is simply this. A great deal of fear has been created in the public mind about the war materials that are being produced in this country in connection with the war in Viet Nam. For the sake of the record and for the knowledge of the Canadian public, the minister's statement today is of considerable importance. Regardless of the earlier part of his oration which, if he will excuse the allusion, sounded very much like a statement from the minister of external affairs-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: From the N.D.P.

-I think the implication of what he said is that Canada should get out of the production of war materials and that the transition from war to civilian production could be made reasonably successfully and without major disruption.

Mr. Chairman, I was pleased to hear about the plants disposed of by the department. We will all be happy when the transfer from wartime operations is completed. I was also pleased to hear that the department had changed its role in terms of defence production. While I presume the department still buys material for the army, it has adopted the Glassco recommendation of bulk purchasing. I assume that this involves a distributive system, which will create new problems. For example, when you buy paper in bulk you have to store it, and I can envisage storage problems for the department.
I have one final question for the minister. If I had any further questions I would ask them of the parliamentary secretary who has sat silent throughout. If I and my colleagues had anything to do with it defence costs would come

down; therefore that particular function of the department would eventually disappear. At the same time, its purchasing activities are going to increase. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is our intention to do so in about one year's time. It will require legislative enactment and the matter does not seem to be terribly urgent. Although progress is being made on the matter I would be glad to receive suggestions for a new name, though not now.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot let the estimates of this department go through without making a brief but none the less strong protest about the way defence contracts have increased so tremendously during the last year. I am afraid that the minister's talk of phasing out military production is not too convincing in view of the number of defence contracts entered into last year. Indeed, instead of military production being phased out it has been going the other way. We have been building up an intricate network of defence production that will be very hard to undo or to turn to civilian use. I am worried about this because it means we must devote a great part of Canadian industry, resources and manpower to the production of war materials for military needs at a time when civilian needs are increasing.
Because it puts the case much better and more succinctly than I could I should like to quote an editorial that appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail. It commences as follows:
It came out almost incidentally. Michael Forestall (P.C. Halifax) was talking about cost control during the Commons debate on supplementary spending estimates for the defence production department, and mentioned a figure of $20 million a ship for four new destroyers the department has on its drawing board.
Not $20 million, corrected defence production minister C. M. Drury, by now it was "a lot closer to $50 million", and maybe more. The ships would be built over four years and changes in naval warfare might dictate design changes at increased cost-
Designed four years ago for service four years hence and dubious service at that. We have yet to redefine our NATO commitments, we can have no certainty that any of our U.N. roles will require such vessels: and if there is one thing most Canadians feel they could do without, it is a ship that fires surface to air missiles. At what?

But four of them will cost us $200 million. There goes $50 million more than will be raised by finance minister Mitchell Sharp's 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporate income taxes for the 1968-69 fiscal year, there goes nearly double the $105 million aid Canada sent to Indian last year- our biggest foreign aid item.
In what strange unreal world does the government live, where it can preach restraint to us and proceed, almost casually, with a huge and open-ended expenditure on what the judgment of Canadians-if it could be totalled up-would almost certainly decide was an unnecessary and even undesirable project?
I think the Globe and Mail has hit the nail on the head. From what I have heard during the last two days it seems we are living in a strange and unreal world. The minister is hoping that we can phase out military needs in order to meet other needs. Certainly the needs of the people of this country are tremendous. They require new housing. There is the problem of pollution control in its various phases. There are requirements for education and training from one coast to the other. There are pension problems both civil and military. The elderly need a pension increase and medicare expenses are coming along. This is why it is so unreal to spend such tremendous sums on defence production. Against what and against whom will these weapons be used?

Our country faces real and growing needs and it is high time we got down to reality and came down to earth. The people of this country are being taxed for services they hope they will receive.
