I welcome the minister's remarks about administrative procedures and I wish to bring to his attention some problems in connection with purchasing which have arisen in various ridings. For instance, in certain ridings where the government purchased automobiles the dealers who were not successful in tendering were very upset and told their member of their dissatisfaction. On the other hand, dealers who were successful in tendering soon found that the service commitments of their contracts meant that they had to spend more in servicing government cars than they would have spent in servicing the general public's cars. In other words, the dealers are damned if they win and damned if they don't. I think there is an obligation on the part of the department to make certain that automobile manufacturers stand behind their dealers. Often the manufacturers dodge their responsibilities and the dealer winds up making nothing or next to nothing.
When a dealer sells a standard Chevrolet, he makes a mark-up of $700, $400 of which is earmarked for service for engines, rear ends or other servicing needs that may arise. Usually the manufacturer stands behind his product but I have been told that some manufacturers have blackmailed local dealers into doing certain work without compensation. Originally the dealer arranged with the manufacturer to be compensated for the work. Actually the dealer got a kickback from the manufacturer for servicing the car, but I have been told that General Motors has stopped giving this kickback to its dealers. I have received many letters and I have heard many opinions expressed about whether General Motors is or is not in some way reimbursing its dealers for work being done.

a high concentration of unemployed, which would have affected them adversely. I wonder whether, in the country as a whole, some areas have not been at a disadvantage due to the system used by the department to designate those areas.
I should like to continue with the description of the role of the department.
In more precise economic terms, the department seeks to attain a dual objective: to raise the level of productivity and to make it possible for our industries to compete on the domestic and foreign markets. Furthermore, its purpose is to prepare and implement programs intended to create new job opportunities and to raise incomes through the industrial development of the areas of Canada which have been designated because of chronic unemployment, underemployment or low incomes.
One or two days ago, in answer to the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain), the minister stated that the areas were not designated by the Department of Industry but rather by the Department of Manpower and Immigration, according to the level of unemployment prevailing in those areas. [DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I fully understand the situation. However, I wonder whether this procedure is fair to all the areas, for in the region in which I am interested, that of Abitibi, there are between 400 and 500 men who have to travel to the province of Ontario to work in lumber camps, sawing wood or transporting it to mills where it is converted and prepared for the market.
These men must travel over a hundred miles to come back to their homes during the weekend, which increases their expenses considerably. Moreover, they cannot be considered as unemployed. In fact, they are not unemployed but must earn a living in an area located in a neighbouring province and designated as an economically depressed area.
Therefore, I think that, in so doing, an injustice is committed against northwestern Quebec, for as far as I know, two lumber processing industries at least would be interested in coming to a northwestern Quebec town, namely La Sarre; but being unable to get any aid under the Designated Areas Act, they will probably settle down in the neighbouring province, where they will be entitled to the subsidies granted in designated areas.
I agree with the hon. minister and the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) that northern Ontario can supply raw materials to this lumber industry. But, I should like to point to

subtopic: LONDON AND MIDLAND GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the sole purpose of this bill is to change the name of this company from London Midland General Insurance Company to Avco General Insurance Company. There are two reasons for the desired change. This company is a member of the Avco group of companies, and the Avco corporation is the parent company of the entire group. Last year there was a company in the United Kingdom which used the names "London" and "Midland" as the main names of that company. It went into bankruptcy and there have been some inquiries as a result. The company has been asked whether there was any connection between these two companies. There is no connection between these two companies whatsoever, but this is the reason for this change.
Let me point out to hon. members that Avco Holding Corporation of Canada is not the sole owner of the London and Midland General Insurance Company. Approximately 50,000 shares are held by Canadian citizens. I hope that hon. members will see lit to allow this change of name, which is all that is being sought.

I do not know whether it will be better off, since I am told the word "Avco" appears in the names of at least six Canadian companies, and that seven companies which include that word in their names operate in the United States.
Though this company seeks to remove the word "London" from its name I doubt whether the name change will accomplish anything. Never having dealt with them, I am not in a position to say. I was also wondering about the significance of remarks by the bill's sponsor, that 50,000 company shareholders live in Canada. That has nothing to do with the company's name, but I wonder if he was trying to say that the change of name will make the company Canadian owned. I hope that was not the intention of his remarks, because the Senate committee report says clearly that this company is a subsidiary of a United States parent which has "Avco" in its name.
We should scrutinize this bill more carefully than some members seem to have done. The Senate committee says the company is changing its name to protect its reputation, and to get away from a similar name that has been associated with a company that went bankrupt. Whether that is the real reason for the change we cannot say. The reasons why entities and persons in society sometimes change their names are not always clear. When a person wants to change his name, either to

escape from the law or for some other reason, he goes before the courts and they decide whether the change can be made. The ordinary person bears his father name. My name is that of my father.

speechtext:
I thought the item before us, 25 c, would provide an appropriate occasion for considering some of the problems which have arisen in connection with the designated area program. What the program really underlines is the inadequacy of the entire Department of Industry and the failure of that department to live up to the high hopes which were held for it.
When I say this, I also want to indicate that I have been much impressed by the staff of the department. In many ways the department has some of the best personnel of any government department. I have on many occasions had the opportunity of consulting them on various questions which have arisen in connection with our local industries and on all those occasions I have found them only too anxious to be of help-and they have been helpful-and to do their best to assist.
The failures as I see them do not stem from any unwillingness on the part of the staff to be helpful but from the fact that frequently, I suspect, they are hamstrung by government policies originating outside the department, including tariff policies designed to protect certain of our large industries. For instance, an attempt to bring in certain kinds of raw or semi-finished material for additional processing in Canada ran into a wall. In these circumstances it is difficult for small companies to get off the ground, as it were. In one case we had an opportunity to assist a small company which needed raw material from the United States. The companies which were able to make this material in Canada did not wish to do so, certainly not in the quantities desired. Yet they behaved like dogs in the manger and stopped the material coming in by using the argument that some day they might choose to make this material, and therefore they needed protection.
The department has been hesitant and cautious in its operations. Too much so, in my opinion. The program began with one set of criteria and then another was introduced. Neither has proved adequate. It seems to me the department is confused about its objectives. I would have thought the Department of Industry would have been primarily interested in the growth of secondary manufacturing in Canada. Unfortunately this has not apparently been the case, despite the fact that our growth in this area has certainly not been adequate in terms of our resources or potential. We have fallen behind other countries in

March 21, 1968
Supply-Industry
our productivity, until at the present time I believe we are in thirteenth or fourteenth place on the list of industrialized nations as far as per capita productivity growth is concerned. Our industrial efficiency has, I feel, been sacrificed for the sake of limiting unemployment in some areas. No one argues against the great need to limit unemployment whenever possible. It is deplorable, and it must be lessened wherever it exists. The question, however, is: Can one correct this situation through a program such as the designated area program? I think the answer must be, no.
Consider the areas which have the highest levels of unemployment, areas which do not have much potential for growth. We can see that the designated area program has not been of great assistance to them. It seems the program has been most successful in introducing industry into areas close to industrial centres. One has the feeling that industries have simply been persuaded by bonuses into locating in areas where they might well have gone anyway.
One of the central problems with which the department should be dealing is the slow rate of increase in productivity. The record in Canada is not good. One recent study indicated that in Canada there was probably 29 per cent more capital invested per worker in secondary manufacturing industry than in the United States, yet despite this our productivity was some 30 per cent lower than productivity south of the border.
I do not think the blame for this can be attributed to labour. I think the responsibility for productivity is a responsibility of management. Even the responsibility of management is limited to a certain extent by the fact that in this country we have an unfortunate, dinky toy industrial structure, modelled on that of the United States, a structure which is inefficient by American standards because of the small size of the domestic market. Yet despite this limitation it contains almost as many competing firms as does the vastly larger United States market.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
There is a need for rationalization of our industries. People in the department are aware of the problem; it is not news to them. They have written on the subject and made speeches on it. They have pointed out the problems in our furniture industry. I understand a study is taking place at present, but I

can find nothing that has been done in the rationalization program.
The minister may reply that a type of rationalization has taken place under the Canada-United States auto agreement. I would agree with him that it is a type of rationalization, but I hope it is the last of this type of rationalization that we will see. Because of the long runs that are necessary, almost continental runs, because of the wide range of lines and choices in automobiles required by the public, when the agreement was made we may not have been in a discretionary position regarding rationalization of the automobile industry; but had we taken action years ago in anticipation of the developing problem, something might have been done. We might have done what European countries did. They developed specialities. They developed particular automobiles suitable for their climate. They exported those to other nations, and in return imported models not available from their own production. In that way we could have established a rational automobile industry. However, that possibility is no longer open to us.
While many of us have been forced to give reluctant approval to the kind of rationalization that took place under the Canada-United States auto agreement, we feel quite strongly that this kind of approach should be dropped. It is sometimes argued that continental integration brings great benefits to Canada. Some of the benefits can be demonstrated; others cannot.
I would like to deal with farm machinery, which for a long time has been an integrated industry. There has been free trade in farm equipment between Canada and the United States, yet it is hard to see that major benefits have resulted from this type of North American integration. A report was prepared for the Massey-Ferguson Company by Hed-land and Menzies, the purpose of which was to demonstrate why Massey-Ferguson could not pay parity wages with the United States. Had I been in a position to make a decision on that report I think I would have hidden it, because its conclusions are frightening.
The argument used to show why Massey-Ferguson cannot have parity wages in Canada is that the company has built its labour intensive factories in Canada and its automated factories in the United States, and if the wage rates were the same it would have to close down its factories in Canada. This may or may not be the case; I am not in a position to
March 21. 1968

judge, but the implication of this must surely shock every Canadian, to think that, after the opportunities for continental integration had been worked out, what the company was doing was placing in its factories in the United States rather than in its factories in Canada, the advantages and benefits to be gained from automation.
The only conclusion that can be drawn from that report is that unless we in Canada are prepared to operate on a permanently lower wage scale there will be few factories in this country. If our goal is to be that Canadians must continue to be placid hewers of wood and drawers of water, then continental integration will permanently condemn Canada to a lower standard of living.
The great need in this country is to find a more rational way of organizing our production. Professor Watkins' task force report, tabled recently, pointed out the fundamental problem of Canadian industry as being too many plants producing too many goods in too small a volume. Others pointed this out previously, but when the question of rationalization is raised everyone begins to picture deserted towns and factories, with this plant shut down and that plant shut down. I suggest that this does not have to be one of the end results of rationalization.
We need more specialization in our plants. Instead of our plants trying to duplicate each other's efforts, trying to make a complete range of products, they could effect economies by specializing in a few items. If this were done, all the plants now in existence could continue to operate. A study made comparing plant sizes in Canada with plant sizes in the United States showed that in many cases Canada had better and larger sized plants than the United States, but in most instances the Canadian plant was producing an infinitely greater range of products than its counterpart across the border.
As I say, the department is aware of this problem. The minister's officials know about it. What are they doing about it, and why are they not proceeding faster with the rationalization program? I would like to believe that the minister and his officials wish to do something about the problem, but are under certain constraints. In personal discussions I have had with the minister he has expressed his concern. He has demonstrated his knowledge and awareness of the problem. In his gentle way he has said to me, "Well, it isn't easy, and it's going to take a long time." We
Supply-Industry
on this side are impatient. We know it is not easy but we are not prepared to accept that it is going to take a long time. I think the time can be shortened if there is sufficient political courage to act.
I hope that before too long some concrete proposals will emanate from the department to solve the lack of specialization and the high costs of our secondary industry. It is not good enough, as some economists suggest, to take away tariff protection from our industries and let them compete internationally. I am sure some of our industries would survive, but given the present structure of Canadian industry as a whole many of them would go down, and go down rapidly. Parent companies in the United States would say, "There is no point in our having a plant in Canada any more. We will simply ship our over production from the United States to Canada." A program other than simple tariff removal has to be developed. Tariff removal could be very useful once the rationalization program is implemented.
Perhaps there should be consultation with the various industries involved. They should be called together. The seriousness of the problem to Canada should be pointed out to them, and they should be asked to suggest some solution. They should be asked to find a way of co-operating with the federal government in achieving what in the long run would be a common objective for themselves and the nation.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
One of the industries under consideration by the department was the furniture industry. About a year ago I read an article which expressed some concern about this industry. I do not remember the exact figures, but something in the neighbourhood of over 1,000 small furniture manufacturing industries are located in small towns, and in many cases they are the only sources of employment. What can be done about a situation of this kind? I think the Department of Industry could act as a marketing board for various small manufacturing firms. This would prevent many of them from duplicating sales efforts. Perhaps the department could act in the same way as do the automobile parts suppliers. It could seek out orders and then inform the various small companies of the orders, so that they in turn could place their bids. This would allow the small companies to specialize, rather than produce a wide range of products at tremendous expense because of tooling costs. I think

March 21, 1968
Supply-Industry
the Department of Industry should give serious consideration to this idea.
Perhaps the efforts of the Canada Development Corporation could be directed toward rationalization of industry, or perhaps that corporation and the Department of Industry could work together in this regard. These are some of the areas I hope the minister and his department will explore. Much of the work of this department seems to be isolated from the work done by other government agencies, provincial departments and their planning agencies. Agencies in the maritimes make recommendations which are negated or frustrated by proposals of the Department of Industry. One of these is the designated area program.
The entire maritime area, with the exception of the main cities of Halifax and Saint John, have been designated. Apparently these two cities are the only places in the maritimes where industrial growth is possible. If the objective of the department is to establish a small industry in every small town, perhaps it is carrying out its function. But if its objective is to foster growth and make sure that potential is realized, then it must change its attitude toward the designated area program. This program will not work out in the long run because various industries grow and then decline.
An example of this type of difficulty can be found in the electronics industry in Nova Scotia. The government of that province has had to bail that industry out of difficulty. As long as we continue to have one or two small industries in our small towns we are not being fair to them. I suggest that we are doing nothing but fooling them. At one time during the course of the debate in respect of the Department of Industry my remarks were not as mild as they are tonight. I referred to the designated area program as a cruel hoax. In this regard we are fooling the people and giving them a false sense of security. Because an industry has been established in a small community, the people look forward to employment and feel there may be a future for their children. Technological advances create rapid growth and rapid decline in industry. Very often the employment that exists today will disappear in the future.
For humanitarian and social reasons I should not like to see the development of a program which would take people away from their homes, and the associations which are important to them. Even if it can be demonstrated that this is the most efficient way of

doing things, there must be some balance between efficiency and humanitarianism. There has to be some balance between social plans and industrial efficiency. One of the areas we should examine, to obtain the maximum benefit from both, is the concept of growth centers. I have in mind specific areas in all parts of Canada which could absorb the surplus working population, and the young people who are moving from the farms and small towns where growth is negligible. In this way employment opportunities could be provided for these people.
It is possible in a city such as Halifax to have a variety of industries. There is stability in this situation, because as one industry declines another may grow; yet the employment opportunities remain about the same. The people who might be moved into Halifax could be moved from other parts of the province and would not be far from their homes or associations. They would be much happier under these circumstances than if they were moved from that province to Vancouver, for instance. Anyone who knows the maritime people is aware of how deep their roots are and how important to them are their associations. With growth centres and long range employment prospects we would have employment opportunities and an improved standard of living.
In some ways the designated area program gives us the worst of two worlds. In a private enterprise system people are supposed to know the best places to locate, because of long range employment prospects. The argument in that regard is being offset by the designated area program because it interferes with that type of planning. These areas do not get the benefits of industrial organization or planning on the basis of growth potential. As a result of this program we see a distortion of industrial planning.
Although this program may have been conceived with the best intentions it simply is not adequate in this country, which is rapidly becoming industrialized and needs greater growth and productivity than now seems to be taking place. It seems to me that the department has been saddled with impossible government decisions. It seems as though the cabinet does not know this department exists or what it is trying to accomplish, and perversely tries to destroy whatever good work it may be doing.
March 21, 1968

[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We had an example of this recently when the Minister of Finance brought in a budget that was intentionally designed, in our opinion, to create unemployment. When you have rising unemployment, such a policy aggravates the situation. If the designated area program is supposed to have been created for the relief of unemployment or to assist in solving the unemployment problem, why is the Minister of Finance trying to create unemployment? These two approaches are self-cancelling, and I am sure frustrating.
The manpower program is not adequate to meet our needs. We have a limited manpower program, especially in the mobility sector, which pays small sums of money to those who wish to move out of certain areas. The money paid is not sufficient to induce people to leave their homes, because when an area starts to decline there is a rapid decline in all aspects of its economy; there is a loss of market for things like housing and the other assets that are built up over the years by the ordinary workingman.
If we are to have a proper mobility program we must be willing to pay adequate sums of money to those who have to be moved. It is not enough to pay a man $500 or $1,000 to leave his home, especially if his home cannot be sold because of a declining market. You have to ensure that he suffers no loss.

I feel very badly, Mr. Chairman, because the first time I rise to take part in this debate somebody invites me to sit down. We have just listened to a very interesting and worth-while speech by the hon. member for Waterloo South who represents in the house a very highly industrialized riding. It is only natural that the remarks I make on this subject will be quite different from those made by the hon. member for Waterloo South, because I represent a very different type of constituency. My area does not have the problem of too much industrialization and all the other complex problems the hon. member brought forward with regard to the interplay between the United States and
Supply-Industry
Canada-subsidiary companies, and so on and so forth. The area I represent would welcome a few of the problems outlined by the hon. member for Waterloo South. If they are very difficult problems to cope with, at least they would be very different from those with which we have always had to cope. As I think most hon. members know, my constituency is what is known in Canada as elephant country; it is an area of vast resources. We have only scratched the surface of some of these resources in the last 50 years. Anybody who knows this country realizes that its potential has scarcely been tapped.
The problems that have developed over the very short history of the north country are not those of overindustrialization but of no industrialization. The problems in this part of the country have been, ever since the first settlement in the area, like those of the milk cow; the produce has been taken away from the area, and that is the last its people have seen of it. It is only in recent years that governments both provincial and federal have seemed to take any cognizance of these facts, and two attempts have been made under the federal program to bring this area within those regions of Canada which need federal attention and assistance.
Unfortunately, as was pointed out so well by the hon. member for Waterloo South, while these programs have made great headlines in the newspapers, as far as the region I represent is concerned they have had very little, if any, effect. In fact under the first designated area program not one industry was induced to open up a business in my constituency. Then the government realized that perhaps the plan was not as effective as it might be and some changes were made. I am sure the minister would like the program to be effective. I do not think it is natural that any minister responsible for a program that received as much attention, headlines and whoop-de-doo as this one, would want it to be a complete failure. I think the minister would very much like this program to be successful and really accomplish something. But unfortunately, even under the changed terms of the program we have yet to see very much effect in the region I represent. I think the reason is quite simple. I do not believe the government has really looked into this area and considered the problems that it has. I do not think the government has made any really serious effort to try to cope with the problems of the area. If the government were

March 21, 1968
Supply-Industry
really interested in its program being successful and carried out any kind of study of the situation, it would find that the first place at which to start dealing with the problems is the transportation field. Many difficulties have been caused by the transportation policy of this country in the last 100 years.
It is quite possible that this policy had some sense at the time it was first introduced-and I am referring specifically to the policy which subsidizes the transportation of raw materials. We dip into the pocket of the taxpayer in order to subsidize the transportation of raw materials from outlying areas to built up areas or foreign markets in the United States, Europe, Asia or somewhere else in the world. Then we try to compensate for this by again dipping into the pocket of the taxpayer, and more particularly into the pocket of the consumers of the north, in order to pay artificially high rates for bringing back finished products.
This has been the history of the north country and other resource areas of Canada. We should appreciate the problem inherent in this situation, because for many years the United States was a country of tremendous raw materials and natural resources; but most of these resources have either been depleted or are within a few years of being totally depleted. Only in the northern part of this hemisphere and the northern part of our country do we have left vast amounts of natural resources. More and more the hungry maw of the manufacturing and processing industries of the United States and the whole North American continent will be looking with covetous eyes at the resources left on this continent. As I said before, these resources are not in the southern part of this country, but they are in the north.
Even in southern Canada, let alone in the rest of this continent, we have built up tremendous problems; problems of pollution, overcrowding, housing and land development. For example in eastern Canada we are even taking away some of the few fruit growing areas that we have left. They are bulldozing the fruit trees out and putting in factories to add to the congestion, the pollution problems, the overcrowding and the housing problems. We have two things in abundance in the great north country:	natural	resources-raw
materials-and all kinds of space. But many years ago we got into the habit of thinking the economical thing to do is to dig out these resources in the north, reach into our pockets to subsidize the raw materials, take them

down south to the factories where the population is, and then dig into our pockets to try to find some way to assist in housing, to clean up pollution, or to do this, that and the other thing.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I wonder if we have ever really looked at the over-all situation and stopped to figure out just what is costly and what is economical. If we do this sensibly, we will find that the so-called programs of assistance for the undeveloped areas, as the hon. member for Waterloo South pointed out, have worked reasonably effectively in areas close to industrial regions. This is the only place where we have seen any really effective result from these programs put out by the federal government.
But it is time we took a closer look at the over-all situation. Let us take a look at the region I represent. We produce gold, copper, zinc, silver, asbestos, iron: You name it, it is there. But what do we do? We ship the copper to the province of Quebec, to Sweden or to Japan. We ship zinc to the United States. We ship silver God knows where. We ship asbestos to the United States over railways which we built and subsidized with the taxpayers' money to provide jobs for people in other countries to process our raw material. Yet we have in the north country the problem of underdevelopment.
The people of the north country are sick and tired, when this problem is brought to the federal attention, of hearing from officials that this is under provincial jurisdiction, and, in turn, of hearing from provincial authorities that there is nothing they can do about it, that this is under federal jurisdiction. They are sick and tired of this game of ping-pong which has been going on for so long. I attended meetings last year where it was suggested, and I know there is a strong feeling that it is time the north country broke away from the rest of Canada. This feeling does not go by provinces, but runs right across northern Manitoba, northern Ontario and northern Quebec, because the people in northern Quebec feel they have far more in common with northern Ontario than they have with Quebec city, and the people of northern Ontario say they have far more in common with the people in Noranda, Rouyn, and Val d'Or than they have with the city of Toronto. The same thing occurs right across the northern resource area. The reason for the great difficulties we are experiencing at this time in
March 21, 1968

holding our country together is this lack of realization and lack of understanding of the problem. This is why our country is in danger of flying apart at the seams. I think it is high time this government, or any government, realized this.

speechtext:
In 1934 to 1944 they saved one province. Perhaps we now have a chance of saving the country.
This is a problem which I would like to draw to the attention of the minister. If he can show me where the present designated area program or the one preceding it has established one industry in this area, I would like to know about it. I have attended meetings at which officials of the department have explained the program and the benefits to be derived from it. It looked very good and the people attending the meetings were very enthusiastic. However, when they looked a little deeper into it they realized it would not work. This program was completely ineffective in areas in which they hoped to develop industries. I think it would be far better if the government devoted its energy, its brains and its time to linking secondary industries to the resources of the north.
Two or three years ago all of us in Canada were very impressed and very pleased by the tremendous discoveries by the Texas Gulf Sulphur Company ten miles north of Timmins which brought in possibly the biggest ore deposit in the world of zinc, copper and silver. By the time this company is fully developed it will be the biggest silver mine in the world, it will certainly be the biggest zinc mine in the world, and if the copper content comes up to expectation it will be one of the biggest copper mines in the world. From the information which I could gather there is a sufficient supply there for the next 75 to 100 years. However, a year after the mine went into production, processing 10,000 tons a day all we saw were trainloads of zinc concentrate being taken south and trainloads of copper concentrate heading for Noranda.
Gold mines were closing down, and I will have some more to say on this when we reach the estimates of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Gold mines are closing down again, as a result of the policy pursued by this government, and the future of this tremendous area is as uncertain now as it was ten years ago. As I said, if the energy, brains
Supply-Industry
and resources of this government were directed toward a sensible policy with regard to the smelting, processing and manufacturing of the ores that are right there, the jobs would be where the ore is. Surely with all the waste contained in the concentrates, it is far more sensible and economical to ship the finished product, particularly in view of the transportation problem in this country of large areas. I am afraid I listened to our own propaganda and believed that when our area became designated the problems of northern Ontario would be solved. I am sorry to say that that is not necessarily true.
The designated areas program has a number of weaknesses, one of them being that it asks for provincial government co-operation. I am always unhappy when the federal government passes legislation that calls for the co-operation of provincial governments, since the legislation can only be as good as the lowest common denominator applicable to it permits it to be. Ontario I am afraid is not interested in development, and in this program the province of Ontario represents the lowest common denominator.
Not long ago we had an election in Ontario and as a result some interesting changes took place in northern Ontario. In particular, I wish to refer to the ridings of Timiskaming and Timmins. In both ridings the election was contested by an N.D.P. candidate and in each campaign the central issue was the need for additional development in northern Ontario and the lack of interest being shown in that development by the province. The Ontario cabinet minister who represented Cochrane South, which included Timmins and Cochrane, is without doubt a most capable

administrator; we shall hear more of him when the greater Ottawa metropolitan area is finally created. Also, he brought a college to the area, not because it was the best area for the college but because he could get the college to the area.
The Ontario cabinet minister fought his election, saying he had done as much as could be expected for his area. Shortly after that election I met the Speaker of the Ontario legislature overseas and I said, "What happened in northern Ontario?" He said, "Well, every time that cabinet minister asked us for something, we gave it to him; he got his new school and hospital-he got whatever he asked for."
I say, Mr. Chairman, that he did not bring to the area what the people of northern Ontario really needed, development. The people in the designated areas want jobs, but there is no potential for the employment of educated men in northern Ontario. Basic industry does not need educated men, except in a limited way; it wants a strong back and a weak mind. Our people in northern Ontario are being well educated; our educational system is as good as southern Ontario's-however good that may be.

One of those taking part is a millionaire who recently moved to Montreal-I suppose he has been there for three years now. He comes from northern Ontario. This man was talking to one of my hon. friends about the desirability of moving from Montreal; he did not find it a good place in which to invest and he was thinking of moving out of the area. He indicated that 600 companies were transferring from Quebec.

I was surprised to And that this was not the way in which industry was flowing now; it was flowing into the state of Vermont to the south. This man is very interested in speculation; he is much concerned about the quality of his investments because he makes his living that way. Industry over there has been refused permission to settle in areas where there is a shortage of social capital, of schools, hospitals, fire departments, police departments, housing, and land for industrial development. Other countries have tackled this problem much more effectively than we have in Canada.

When the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs met after Christmas it studied the Kennedy round agreements, and the implications to Canadian manufacturers, industry, labour and agriculture. The Prime Minister made a statement to the effect that there would be help for manufacturers in three main areas; by government insured loans, by direct loans and by shared agreement in respect of consultative services provided by the government. When he made that statement he said $10 million would be available for industry. Last year when the Minister of Finance presented his budget he said we must fight inflation by the traditional methods of taxation and cutting down on government expenditures. He was roundly applauded by the Conservative opposition when he suggested we should cut down on government expenditure. A short time later the President of the Treasury Board set forth in an hour-long discourse what those cutbacks would be. I think the government is going too far in cutting the promised $10 million to $1.
The purpose of the adjustment assistance program was to help manufacturers only. We in this party believe this is gross discrimination. Other ministers informed the committee that labour would get some support through additional benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. It was stated that before insurance was granted there would be some 27053-499
Supply-Industry
protection for the employees, in that the companies would have to give notice before any layoff. These were the only two items set forth in respect of labour.
The Minister of Industry and other ministers were questioned about this situation and it was obvious that they had not consulted with labour prior to entering into the Kennedy round negotiations. There was no consultation during the negotiations and none as a result of the negotiations. Therefore labour was completely left out and workers were forced to accept whatever small help would be provided under the increase in unemployment insurance benefits.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We spoke to members representing the agricultural industry. I asked them direct whether any government officials had consulted representatives of agriculture with regard to the Kennedy round negotiations. The answer was that prior to the negotiations there had been rather informal discussions with representatives of the agricultural industry, but during and after the discussions on the Kennedy round these representatives were not consulted.
The main bodies representing agriculture and industry were almost totally ignored by the government with regard to the effects of the Kennedy round negotiations. The only group the government is concerned with are the manufacturers. That is the reason the minister brings forth this item this evening, in order to help manufacturers in certain areas. The minister says: As a result of the Kennedy round we would like to restructure their operations. They may be seriously injured. That is the first ground. Second, the minister says that as a result of the Kennedy round negotiations there may be export opportunities with regard to which we should assist manufacturers. This is the help the minister is prepared to give industry to get it over the difficulty that has arisen as a result of the Kennedy round.
There was no consultation with labour, very limited consultation with agriculture, but full consultation and participation with the representatives of industry. That is the attitude adopted by the government with regard to this very serious problem. There are several questions I should like to ask the minister. The first is why we have this item of $1, when the Prime Minister said at the time that the government would make $10

March 21, 1968
Supply-Industry
million available. I should like to know why the minister is setting up an insurance fund under which the government will guarantee loans that manufacturers obtain either from approved lenders of the government or direct from the government. Why is it necessary that the government act as a lender of last resort in assisting manufacturers? One would think manufacturers could go to the banks and other lending institutions and make arrangements with regard to the changes that will take place as a result of the Kennedy round, without having to depend upon the government to insure loans they obtain through the banks and other lending institutions.
Why cannot the banks themselves, which have shown enormous profits in recent years-it has been a continual pattern of increasing profits for banks-take some of the risk in this matter? Why should loans they make be insured by the government? This means that if a manufacturer cannot keep up the payments on a loan, the government will step in. Surely if the government is going to step in it will cost more than the $1 provided in these supplementary estimates.
I should like the minister to make a statement about how much he anticipates this program will cost. I know that according to the item the loans will continue for a period of five years. A projection should be made by the high priced officials in the minister's department, who are always ready to guide and service him with regard to these problems, as to the cost of the program. The minister should tell us what the actual cost will be.
We should also have from the minister a statement with regard to the interest rates that banks and lending institutions will be allowed to charge in respect of these loans. The government is to be the lender of last resort, much like the Industrial Development Bank. We know that the Industrial Development Bank is a lender of last resort for industries which cannot obtain loans direct from the chartered banks. We know that the interest rates of the Industrial Development Bank are a little higher than those of the banks. Surely the minister should place some limitation on the interest rates that will be chargeable by the banks in respect of loans which will be insured by the government. I think we should be given the answers to these questions.
When the minister appeared before the committee he gave a very glowing report of

how beneficially Canadian manufacturers will be affected as a result of the Kennedy round. He was all encouragement to the manufacturers, but he forgot to mention that the government has made a value judgment and is going to depend upon the development of secondary industry, much to the detriment of Canadian manufacturers in the development of exports. This is one matter he did not really develop in his report to the committee.
Another matter on which the minister should give us more enlightenment is whether he is prepared, even at this late stage, to consider the TAB, the transitional assistance benefits, payments which some industries received when the Canada-United States auto pact came into play. I think he should give us the reasons for the TAB program not applying to the Kennedy round negotiations in respect of labour. When one considers the shabby treatment labour has received as a result of these negotiations, the least the minister and the government can do is set forth a TAB program to help workers who will suffer as a result of the Kennedy round negotiations.
These are some of the problems with which the minister should deal. When I questioned him about the Canada-United States auto pact he waxed eloquent and said what a wonderful pact it has been. However, he dealt quite lightly with the problem of parity of prices as a result of the Kennedy round. I should like to hear what the minister has to say about this policy.
Mr. Chairman, it is ten o'clock. Perhaps the minister wants the evening to prepare the answers to some of the questions that have been asked.

INCOME TAX ACT-INQUIRY AS TO EXAMINATION AND APPROVAL BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week B.S.A., before the silly age, set in, I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) a question on March 13 which may be found at page 7587 of Hansard. I asked him whether he had examined and approved the tax bill ruled upon Monday in this house. The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, this is a question of departmental administration. I am not sure that I am required to answer it under the rules.
I wish to suggest this evening that this is not a matter of departmental administration but a question of ministerial responsibility. I will refer to the Bill of Rights, chapter 44 of the acts of parliament of 1960. Section 3 reads as follows:
The Minister of Justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the Privy Council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons-
What it boils down to is that section 3 requires that the Minister of Justice examine every bill introduced in the House of Commons. Apart from the requirements of the Bill of Rights, I think it would be obvious that it is the duty of the Minister of Justice to examine every piece of government legislation. After all, he is the chief law officer in this place and the chief legal adviser of the government, and unless times have changed drastically, he is probably head of the cabinet legislative committee, which at least existed under former administrations and I suppose also exists under the present one.
The minister's answer seems to me to suggest that it was the duty of his departmental officials and not of himself to examine the particular legislation, the taxation measure part of which was found out of order. I suggest that in a parliamentary democracy a minister cannot hide behind public servants or his officials. Indeed I suggest that the reverse is true, and that public servants are entitled to every last ounce of protection that a minister can give them. I find the answer 27053-4991
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion even stranger when it comes from a man who aspires to the highest office, the head of the government of this country with 200,000 or more public servants to speak for.
Perhaps there are some reasons for it. The minister in chapter 2 of his "Canadian Charter of Human Rights" tends to make light of the Bill of Rights. He properly points out that it is not enshrined in our constitution, that therefore it can be repealed, and thus is subject to the whim of any parliament. This is true. The Bill of Rights brought in in 1960 could be changed by act of parliament and could be repealed. But until parliament deals with it, I suggest that the minister's responsibility is to carry out every last provision of the Bill of Rights, to be its champion and protector; and above all, if the Bill of Rights tells the Minister of Justice or anyone else in the cabinet to do something, then that minister should hop to it and do exactly what the Bill of Rights tells him to do.
I am driven to make these remarks for two reasons. First, I think the minister has an obligation under the law to do what the law in fact directs him to do. We all recall some rather amusing answers given by ministers of justice in former years when asked whether they read all the provisions of the simple divorce bills which used to bedevil us. Ministers of justice at that time used to say stoutly that they had to see that individual rights were protected. No measure, whether it deals with the plight of specific individuals or deals with larger measures such as the taxes that are imposed on all of us, should escape the eagle eye of the Minister of Justice, if he is doing his duty.
The second reason I rise at this time to make the point arises from a sense of fair play. I believe the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has been pilloried unmercifully, particularly by the members of his own party, for the venture he was forced to embark upon when his taxation measure fell. It seems to me that the Minister of Justice, in his rather cavalier answer, should not be allowed to escape the fact that not only had he part of the collective responsibility for the health and welfare of that measure, but also he had a particular duty under the Bill of Rights to examine the measure to ascertain whether Canadian taxpayers, for example, were being put in double jeopardy in the sense that the issue had been decided one way, and then some attempt was being made to reverse that decision. For these two reasons, one a sense

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of fair play and the other that the minister had a duty under the Bill of Rights, I have been moved to make these few remarks this evening.

WINTER WORKS-INQUIRY AS TO PROJECT AT DESBIENS, P.Q.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 19 I took the liberty of
i[Mr. McCleave.l

directing the following question to the hon. Minister of Manpower and Immigration, as reported on page 7793 of Hansard.
What was the answer given by the minister to the letter sent to him by the mayor of Desbiens, on March 15, with regard to a winter work project estimated at $40,000?
I do not know whether the minister or his parliamentary secretary have on hand the letter signed by the mayor of Desbiens, a small municipality in my district, who is complaining, and rightly so, about the attitude of the federal government, and particularly of the Department of Manpower and Immigration, which appears discriminatory towards him. __
The reasons on which the request of the mayor of Desbiens was based can be summarized as follows: That municipality has some 2,000 inhabitants, 4 or 5 of whom are farmers. This means that the remainder of the population is made up of labourers who, in part, are working at the St. Raymond paper mill. Now, since that paper mill has been operating at about 60 per cent of capacity, about 100 persons have been out of work for some time.
In December last, I understand that the municipality of Desbiens submitted a winter work project amounting to $28,000 but it was reduced by half. I do not know if the provincial or the federal government is responsible, but that project was reduced to $14,000. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, it was not an exorbitant amount to help 100 unemployed.
The municipal council then submitted another winter works program for $40,000; it was flatly turned down by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It was claimed that the program did not meet the standards of the act. But, on reading very closely the letter to the mayor of Desbiens, one can rightly wonder whether all the neighbouring municipalities had met the legal requirements. I do not want to insinuate anything unkind about those municipalities, like Cham-bord and Saint-Jerome, for instance, which carried out winter works programs worth $80,000 and $75,000 respectively, while Desbiens was limited to $14,000.
I sincerely believe that the request addressed to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration by the mayor of Desbiens is motivated, and I am willing to state positively that the department showed a lack of distributive fairness in allotting the winter works program.
As I said a while ago, I do not want to insinuate anything unkind about Chambord
March 21, 1968

or Saint-Jerome, but it is still permissible to
make comparisons.
Mr. Speaker, I protest energetically against the discrimination shown in the case of Des-biens, and I beg the hon. minister to revise his decision which deprives that municipality of the help to which it is entitled, on the same footing as neighbouring municipalities.

speakeroldname: Hon. B. S. Mackasey (Minister without Portfolio):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention to the representations made by the hon. member on behalf of one of the municipalities in the province of Quebec. I was very pleased he stressed that he was not insinuating that there was any malpractice on the part of the department, or that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) was favouring one municipality over another. The hon. member was quick to emphasize this, so it is obvious that the decision in favour of one municipality as opposed to another must have been based on some criterion other than that of political patronage or favouritism of one sort or another.
I do not have the criteria in front of me but I am familiar with the winter works program. I was an alderman in the city of Verdun, in the province of Quebec, and I do know what an important role winter works projects play in some municipalities. If the municipality of Desbiens was refused a winter works project, then I am sure there must have been a logical reason. I do not think the hon. member can make much of a case if he pleads that some municipalities have received winter works they are not necessarily entitled to. For the most part the department applies the same criterion in each case.
I shall bring to the attention of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration tomorrow the particular case of this municipality and recommend that their application be reviewd, so that at least we can tell the hon. member the reason it was refused. I shall speak to the minister, if not tomorrow, then as early as Monday and try to ascertain why this particular project was refused and why similar projects in nearby municipalities were accepted.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon in the unavoidable and understandable absence of the Secretary
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) I asked the hon. gentleman's parliamentary secretary whether the minister had been informed by the government of British Columbia of the expenditure to date on the Columbia river project. I am glad to have the opportunity to deal with this question for a few minutes because some persons in my riding who are staunch supporters of the Liberal party have asked me to raise it, as have some supporters of the Tory party and of my own party. So I am strictly non-partisan on this issue.
I wish to deal briefly with the sequence of events. On April 13, 1962 the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) wrote the following letter to the secretary of the water resources committee of the chamber of commerce of Nakusp: Dear Mr. Waterfield:
Your letter of April 12th has just arrived and I would like to assure you that it is imperative to renegotiate the Columbia river treaty.
May I also assure you that all B.C. interests, particularly those of the water resources committee of Nakusp Chamber of Commerce, will be consulted by a new Liberal government before a final decision is reached.
Kindest regards,
Yours sincerely,
L. B. Pearson
The Prime Minister sent the Secretary of State for External Affairs to undertake this chore for him. Need I add that the water resources committee of the chamber of commerce at Nakusp never saw the hon. gentleman at all; he completely overlooked them in his trip down the river on behalf of the Prime Minister. To indicate how much faith was placed in the Secretary of State for External Affairs I would remind hon. members that in 1965 the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), then minister of labour, had this to say addressing a Columbia river treaty ceremony on Thursday, May 20:
While there are many who deserve credit for what has been made possible, there is one man who perhaps was most responsible for the project going through. This is Paul Martin, who took over the negotiations at the time I spoke of when it looked as if the great gains made by the previous negotiations might be lost, and who proceeded to work so closely with Premier Bennett and his colleagues and with the United States representatives. It was this close association, marked by an atmosphere of determination and good-will, that made possible the results reflected in this ceremony here today.
Apparently this close association and this determination on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs was not enough for
March 21. 1968
7932	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Mr. Bennett, because I read in the Vancouver Sun of Thursday, May 11, 1967:
Asked for his opinion of the treaty, he said: "The treaty missed out. The thing that's at fault In the treaty is that it was signed too quickly."
He blamed federal authorities.
He was referring, of course, to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and expressing dissatisfaction with the hon. gentleman's role in this affair. He recognized him as the key man. The report continues:
Bennett said the arrangement made with Kaiser Aluminum for a dam on the Arrow lakes "was three times better than the treaty".
Imagine that.
The deal concerned the proposed construction in 1954 by Kaiser Aluminum or a $25 million dam on the Arrow lakes. It was championed by former Lands Minister Robert Sommers.
Here is the premier of British Columbia expressing serious dissatisfaction with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs had done in signing this treaty.
I might say that upon being questioned in the external affairs committee on Friday, April 10, 1964, Mr. MacNabb, now a deputy minister, gave certain assurances when asked about the costs of the project. I asked him whether he was sure that his estimate of the cost was correct. The question reads:
In view of the experience of British Columbia Hydro over a number of years-of course their projects would be much smaller than these-we know that the average exceeded the estimated cost by 50 per cent. I have figures supplied by a friend in the British Columbia Hydro. In view of that, what do you think of the assurance that these costs will not greatly increase over the next ten years?
In reply, both Mr. MacNabb and the Secretary of State for External Affairs assured us that the cost had been so accurately estimated that they would have $55 million left over with which to put generators into the Mica Creek dam. Later on, the Secretary of State for External Affairs paid tribute to Mr. MacNabb as a man who knew exactly what he was talking about.
I find, however, on reference to the votes and proceedings of the legislature of British Columbia for Thursday, March 14, that Mr. Strachan asked the premier a number of questions, among which was the following:
With reference to the payment of $274,800,000 received October 1, 1964, under the Columbia river treaty, was any of this money expended to December 31, 1967?
[Mr. Herridge.j

I will not go into the other details of the questions. Mr. Bennett replied as follows:
Yes. Duncan Storage, $30,090,387; Arrow storage, $144,119,555; Mica storage, $85,184,179; general development costs, $1,818,502; total including interest during construction and overhead, $261,212,623.
The government of British Columbia has now practically admitted that the figures which were vouched for by the minister and by Mr. MacNabb are inaccurate and that the government of British Columbia is being obliged to spend over $200 million more than was provided in the treaty signed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs was in Castlegar he addressed members of the Castlegar chamber of commerce at which time he assured them that the government of Canada-
-would not sign any treaty with the United States which did not provide sufficient money to pay for all the costs of construction of Columbia river projects in Canada.
These various gentlemen whom I have mentioned earlier want this question answered. They are extremely interested in it. I am glad the parliamentary secretary is here this evening; I apologize for keeping him out of bed. I hope that when he comes to reply he will answer this question. In conclusion let me say that in the joint engineering board reports Mr. MacNabb never refers once to the total expenditures on the Columbia to date. I should like the parliamentary secretary to tell me whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs has received these figures and, if not, why not.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his remarks tonight the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has inferred that Canada got a poor deal out of the Columbia river treaty. The authorities, the people competent not only in the fields of engineering and finance, but also economists, differ with this view. Canada did in fact get a good deal out of the Columbia river treaty.
I have time tonight to refer to only one authority, a world renowned authority, Dr. John V. Krutilla. In a book entitled "The Columbia River Treaty" published late last year by the well known independent organization, Resources for the Future Incorporated, he said:
The benefit-on the order of $225 million to $275 million-can be regarded as the benefit to Canada from the Columbia River Treaty.
March 21. 1968

This, he said, is-
-measured by the savings in cost as compared with alternatives available to Canada.
I want to stress the fact that he said it is a savings in cost of $275 million. Dr. Krutilla, interestingly enough, did not think that the United States negotiators did anything like as good a job for the United States as the Canadian negotiators did for Canada. He went on to say:
After considering the problem of meeting the power supply and flood management objectives by such means as developing domestic storage and the Northwest-Southwest inter-tie, we find that the Columbia river treaty results in a relative loss to the United States of about $250 million to $375 million.
To recap, Dr. Krutilla is saying that Canada, as a result of the Columbia river treaty, is about one quarter of a billion dollars better off. The United States, on the other hand, will have lost at least a quarter of a billion dollars as compared with other alternatives. If I have a moment, Mr. Speaker, I would
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion like to quote one further short paragraph from his book.
There is no doubt-
-said this world renowned authority-
-that Canada figured with a very sharp pencil. Analysis was used to illuminate policy choices and to evaluate the magnitudes in the trade-offs when economic and political, long run and short run, and similar conflicting objectives were being weighed in the balance-
Whatever its origin, maintenance of the distinction between technical analysis and policy choice was an outstanding Canadian accomplishment.
This is a world wide authority's opinion on the Columbia river treaty.
